title: A smaller field with more MU, simple example

steps.c: G lies inside F. Which of the two fields earns more MU?

Both fields stand on the same ground. Imagine a big square cell made of four quarters. One quarter is a city with 1,000 MU per km². The other three are empty (0). The density of a cell is the MU per km² it holds.
F is big, so it has to use the whole big cell. Its density is the mean of its four quarters, 250. F covers 5.0 km², so it earns 1,250 MU. Most of that area is empty, but the city is averaged into it.
G is small enough to use the city quarter on its own, with density 1,000. G covers 1.8 km², so it earns 1,800 MU: more than F, although G is smaller and lies inside F.
Same city, different cell. F counts it at 250 because F has to use a big cell. G counts it at 1,000 because G can use a small one. Bigger fields have to use bigger cells.
